children.text: of the Bangui Bay coastline, forming Southeast Asia's first commercial wind farm. The sight of a wave-swept beach paired with white windmills has become a signature scene of northern Ilocos, and it's a must-stop landmark on the way to Pagudpud.
Bangui Windmills is a wind farm built along the Bangui Bay coast, in front of the town of Bangui in Ilocos Norte. The first phase of 15 turbines began commercial operation in
, and a second phase of 5 turbines was added in

, completing the 20 turbines lined along the coast. It is known as the first wind power plant in the Philippines and the first in Southeast Asia to start commercial operation, and the 20 turbines on the coast are 1.65 MW machines from Denmark's Vestas. In
a third phase added 6 turbines of the 3 MW class, bringing the installed capacity of the whole complex to about 52 MW today.
Each windmill is overwhelming in scale. The hub tower stands about
in diameter, and standing right beneath one, the loud whoosh of the blades cutting through the air echoes overhead. These giant windmills line up in a row along about
of coastline, so that from one end of the beach, it looks as if white giants are marching endlessly toward the sea.

Bangui sits at the northwestern corner of Luzon, facing head-on into the northeast monsoon (amihan) blowing off the South China Sea. This geography, with strong winds year-round, is why the wind farm was built here, and even larger wind farms later went up on the hills of neighboring Burgos and Pagudpud, making Ilocos Norte something of a symbol of renewable energy in the Philippines.
Seeing the windmills themselves takes about

, but along the coast road from Laoag up to Pagudpud, it's visited as a key stop on the "northern tour," alongside Kapurpurawan Rock Formation and Cape Bojeador Lighthouse. It suits travelers who enjoy driving and photography, and families who want to show their children renewable energy in action.
The spacing between turbines is about

, and in the early days of operation the wind farm is said to have supplied about 40% of Ilocos Norte's electricity demand. ACEN, the renewable energy company of the Ayala Group, which is the majority shareholder of the operator NorthWind, carried out an overhaul project on the mechanical and electrical equipment of all 20 original turbines in two phases over
. In neighboring Burgos, a large wind farm of 50 turbines of the 3 MW class (150 MW) went up in
, and a 27-turbine (81 MW) wind farm stands on the hills of Mount Caparispisan in Pagudpud.

blocks.title: View the row of windmills from the beach

children.text: Head down to the beach from the viewing area and look straight ahead as the windmills recede along the coastline. This perspective-filled shot is the classic photo of the Bangui Windmills.
Get close to the tower and look up, and the
height and the size of the blades become real. On windy days, you can feel the sound and vibration of the spinning blades in your body.

blocks.title: Full views from the roadside overlook

children.text: From the turn-off leading down to the wind farm from the coast road, and from the nearby hillside road, you can look down on the entire row of windmills. It's a good spot to pull over during your drive and take a panoramic photo.
The coast runs a long way east to west facing the sea to the north, so the sun sets beyond the western end of the row of windmills. From
the sun sets over the sea, and from
it sets toward the Burgos hills to the west. If you're staying in Pagudpud, it's worth coming back down in the late afternoon.
Around the entrance are stalls selling windmill-shaped keychains, Inabel textiles, and Ilocano snacks. Miniature windmill models are a popular souvenir sold only here.

blocks.title: Compare with the Burgos and Pagudpud wind farms

children.text: The large wind farm on the hills of Burgos and the one around Mount Caparispisan in Pagudpud stand on grassland and hills, giving off a different mood from the Bangui windmills standing on the beach. Compare them through the car window as you go along on your northern tour.
Bangui beach is a mix of grayish-brown sand and smooth pebbles. Walking slowly among the windmills while listening to the waves roll the pebbles is more atmospheric than you'd expect.

Sentinela Hill in San Lorenzo, Bangui town, is said to be the site of a watchtower used to keep watch for pirate ships during the Spanish era, and a brick tower stands at the top. From the hill you can look down on Bangui town and the Bangui Bay coastline. It is about
by car from the windmill beach, so it's a good stop on the way back.

especially, the strong northeast monsoon makes the windmills spin powerfully, and clear skies bring out a sharp contrast between the blue sky and white windmills. However, the wind is very strong, lowering the felt temperature and blowing sand around, so bring a light windbreaker.
, the wind eases but the sunshine gets stronger. Some days the windmills turn slowly or stand still, but the sea is calm and the sky color is lovely, so photos still come out well.
rainy season is affected by the southwest monsoon and typhoons. According to Laoag observations, monthly rainfall reaches 400–600 mm in

, and the northern tip of Luzon, where Bangui is located, often lies in typhoon paths. When a typhoon warning is issued, access to the beach is restricted, and the Patapat Viaduct section on the way to Pagudpud may also be closed due to landslide risk. In
, a state of calamity was even declared in Ilocos Norte because of Super Typhoon Nando (Ragasa).

Bangui town doesn't have much lodging, so it's common to stay at a beach resort in Pagudpud, about
to the north, or in downtown Laoag and visit on a day trip. Resorts priced around
per night cluster around Saud Beach and Blue Lagoon in Pagudpud, and budget guesthouses start from around

The stalls at the windmill entrance sell simple drinks and snacks. It's better to eat at restaurants in Bangui town or at your resort in Pagudpud. Besides Ilocano staples like bagnet and pinakbet, the coastal villages of northern Ilocos also serve seafood dishes such as inihaw (grilled fish caught that day), tangy seaweed salad, and kilawin (vinegar-cured raw fish). The town of Pasuquin to the south is famous for its crisp biscuit biscocho, a good snack to pick up along the way.

Choose where to stay to fit your itinerary. Laoag is close to the airport, the bus terminal, and restaurants, and it's where the northern tour vans depart from, so it's convenient for trips that cover several sights in a day. Pagudpud is about

from the windmills, so it's good for seeing them at sunset or early morning, and you can enjoy swimming too. At the entrance to the windmill beach and along the hill road to the west, nipa-roofed stalls and rest areas line up, where you can buy drinks, snacks, and souvenirs and take a short break.
The windmills are a short way down from the coast road. If using public transport, tell the driver in advance to let you off at the "windmills."
The wind on the beach is very strong. Wear a hat with a chin strap, tie up long hair, and bring a light windbreaker.

To fit the whole row of windmills in frame, a wide-angle lens or your phone's 0.5x lens is useful. Shooting the line of windmills at an angle from the end of the beach brings out the perspective nicely.
In the morning, the windmills glow white without backlighting, and late in the afternoon is good for sunset silhouettes. Time your visit to match the shot you want.
There are almost no ATMs around Bangui. Bring cash from Laoag for tricycles, souvenirs, and snacks.
Chartering a van for the northern tour lets you cover Kapurpurawan Rock Formation, Cape Bojeador Lighthouse, the Bangui Windmills, the beaches of Pagudpud, and the Patapat Viaduct all in one day.
If you're staying in Pagudpud, come back at sunset. You'll get photos with a completely different mood from daytime.

The wind farm has no night lighting, so the beach and access road quickly get dark after sunset. After shooting the sunset, return straight to your vehicle or a tricycle you have kept waiting, and keep some battery so you can turn on your phone's flashlight.
During Holy Week (the week before Easter) and the
holidays, northern tour vans and Pagudpud resorts fill up early. At these times, book lodging and a vehicle in advance, and see the windmills in the early morning when there are fewer tour groups.
On the beach, some people offer horseback rides among the windmills. Agree clearly on the time and price before riding, and have a guardian walk beside any child.
Bangui beach is for viewing the scenery, not for swimming. Enjoy swimming and bathing at Saud Beach or Blue Lagoon in Pagudpud instead.
Bangui beach has strong waves and areas where the seabed drops off sharply, so it's not suited for swimming. Enjoy it only by wading in up to your feet.
Climbing the turbine towers or writing graffiti on the facilities is prohibited. Since this is a power generation facility, do not enter restricted areas.
Flying a drone may be restricted near the power facility, and the strong wind also poses a high risk of crashing. Follow on-site guidance.
There's almost no shade at midday. Bring a hat, sunscreen, and water.
During typhoon season, approaching the coast is dangerous. Check the weather bureau's forecast, and postpone your visit if a warning is issued.
, sand and fine gravel get blown about and can hurt your eyes and camera lens. Wear sunglasses, and change lenses inside the car.
